video_title: MacroVoices #560 Daniel Lacalle: “The European ER AH Situation…”
gist: After a market 'bloodbath', Tresis chief economist Daniel Lacalle (captioned 'Daniel Lay') argues AI capex is a dispersion risk not a bubble, sees oil settling near $70 WTI as the geopolitical premium erodes, calls the US dollar the 'least bad' fiat currency, says the euro's end game is debasement rather than break-up, and views the gold crash as a buying opportunity. Patrick Ceresna's market desk proposes a call-hedged short on March 2027 Euro FX futures and warns the selling in equities and gold is likely not over (S&P 6,900 test, gold 3,300 support).

insights.claim: Daniel Lacalle argues the AI capex boom is not a bubble but a dispersion problem: some of the largest hyperscalers will be generating net cash in 2027 and can repay their debt, while other AI spenders will suffer declining margins or weak returns.
insights.speaker: Daniel Lacalle
insights.so_what: Favor selectivity (long cash-generative hyperscalers vs. weaker AI capex spenders) over blanket AI exposure or blanket shorts.
insights.quote: when we look at the capital expenditure of the hyperscalers in the case of uh some of the largest ones, they're going to be generating net cash in 2027 and they will be able to repay their debt

insights.claim: Lacalle says the market is currently unable to distinguish AI winners from losers and is selling all AI-linked names in unison, which should resolve into differentiation around the next earnings season.
insights.speaker: Daniel Lacalle
insights.so_what: Indiscriminate AI selling may create mispricings in higher-quality names ahead of next earnings season.
insights.quote: The market right now is unable to decide which one is which and is basically just considering everything in in unison.

insights.claim: Lacalle contends that because the AI bubble is debated constantly, the risk is already embedded in equity valuations and in the yields required on AI-related bonds, which argues against a classic bubble.
insights.speaker: Daniel Lacalle
insights.so_what: Suggests AI-related credit spreads already carry a risk premium; watch the next couple of months for clarification.
insights.quote: it's not a bubble precisely because we're talking about it all the time

insights.claim: Lacalle says data-center moratoria are a political rather than corporate risk: counting both capex overspend risk and moratoria-driven non-deployment double counts the risk, and blocked data centers will simply be built elsewhere.
insights.speaker: Daniel Lacalle
insights.so_what: Moratoria shift where AI investment, jobs and revenues land rather than whether they happen; states imposing them lose out.
insights.quote: if you have on the one hand the concerns about the capital expenditure and on the other hand that capital expenditure is not going to be deployed then obviously you're double counting the risk

insights.claim: If US jurisdictions block data centers, Lacalle expects them to be built in Mexico, North African countries, Asia and parts of Latin America that have ample power capacity and more benign regulation.
insights.speaker: Daniel Lacalle
insights.so_what: Potential beneficiaries are power-rich jurisdictions near the US (Mexico) and North Africa; watch for data-center investment flows there.

insights.claim: Lacalle expects choppy, volatile markets in both technology stocks and sovereign bonds until there is clarity on the Fed's rate path, with a December hike likely adding further volatility.
insights.speaker: Daniel Lacalle
insights.so_what: The December Fed decision is the key near-term catalyst for both tech equities and bonds.
insights.quote: If they increase rates in December, we may have further volatility.

insights.claim: Lacalle attributes the steep correction in energy markets to an erosion, but not disappearance, of the geopolitical risk premium, rejecting both a benign view and the 1973-style crisis some analysts predicted at the start of the Iran war.
insights.speaker: Daniel Lacalle
insights.so_what: Some residual risk premium should stay in oil; neither tail scenario is the base case.

insights.claim: Gulf producers proved far more flexible than expected at recovering volumes and offsetting Iran-related supply risk, which Lacalle calls a significant surprise for many market participants.
insights.speaker: Daniel Lacalle
insights.so_what: Spare-capacity response capped the oil spike; expect similar dampening on future disruptions.

insights.claim: Lacalle forecasts oil settling around $68-70 WTI, ruling out both $30 and $200 per barrel.
insights.speaker: Daniel Lacalle
insights.so_what: Provides a fair-value anchor for oil positioning and energy equity valuations.
insights.quote: not being overly optimistic and thinking that we're going to see oil prices at $30 a barrel but certainly not 200

insights.claim: Lacalle says a US-China-Russia commitment to guarantee supply of refined products is a big change, showing the two largest energy producers (US and Russia) will cooperate to provide security of supply to China.
insights.speaker: Daniel Lacalle
insights.so_what: Great-power coordination on energy supply lowers tail risk for refined product prices.

insights.claim: China has the largest exposure to a Strait of Hormuz closure because 80% of the volumes through the strait go to Asia, which made it both a defender of and integral to the solution.
insights.speaker: Daniel Lacalle
insights.so_what: China's incentive to keep Hormuz open makes it a stabilizing force on Gulf supply risk.

insights.claim: Asked how refined-product cooperation works if refineries keep being attacked, Lacalle concedes it is a vague promise unless Ukraine stops hitting Russian refineries, but argues the US can steer Ukraine away from refineries and China can deter Iran from striking Gulf refineries; he notes China is the second largest investor in Ukraine.
insights.speaker: Daniel Lacalle
insights.so_what: Continued refinery strikes would be the signal that the supply agreement is failing and crack spreads could reprice.
insights.quote: if Ukraine continues to attack Russian refineries then there's no cooperation possible. You it's basically a vague promise.

insights.claim: Lacalle reads point four of the agreement (non-nuclear proliferation) as implying China and Russia agree Iran will not get a nuclear weapon.
insights.speaker: Daniel Lacalle
insights.so_what: If correct, reduces a major tail risk embedded in the Middle East oil premium.

insights.claim: Lacalle names the United States and China as the big winners of the US-China-Russia energy agreement and the OPEC plus response to the Hormuz problem, while Europe sees limited consumer relief because heavy taxation dominates final gasoline prices.
insights.speaker: Daniel Lacalle
insights.so_what: Lower crude helps US and Chinese demand more than European consumers; relative growth favors US/China.

themes.theme: Why the US-Europe gas spread persists

insights.claim: Lacalle expects European natural gas prices to stay well above pre-2022 levels because Ukraine-war disruptions persist, alternatives are not feeding through, and Germany's decision to shut down nuclear left Europe dependent on imported gas.
insights.speaker: Daniel Lacalle
insights.so_what: Structurally high European energy costs remain a drag on European industry and growth.
insights.quote: the misguided decision of Germany to shut down nuclear, the dependence on imported natural gas, those two things have not improved in any shape or form the situation for Europe

insights.claim: Lacalle argues the long-predicted convergence of US and European natural gas prices via LNG exports will not happen because US producers always prioritize domestic consumption and transport costs are too high for clean arbitrage.
insights.speaker: Daniel Lacalle
insights.so_what: Don't bet on US natgas prices rising on export growth; the US-Europe spread can stay wide.
insights.quote: I find it very very difficult to see natural gas prices in the United States going up because of higher exports to Europe

insights.claim: US LNG is the marginal supplier to Europe, bought only after Algerian, Nigerian, Norwegian and Russian gas are exhausted, which lets sellers earn large margins on a small share of volumes.
insights.speaker: Daniel Lacalle
insights.so_what: US LNG exporters' profitability is tied to European supply shortfalls, not to setting the gas price.

insights.claim: Even after the liquefaction buildout, LNG is only about 15% of the total natural gas market, so it does not dictate the molecule's price.
insights.speaker: Daniel Lacalle
insights.so_what: Explains why regional gas price differentials persist despite LNG growth.
insights.quote: it is only 15% of the total market

themes.theme: Dollar: least-bad fiat, Fed overreliance on rates

insights.claim: Lacalle attributes the dollar index's push toward 104 to Fed rate hikes creating a 'vacuum effect' and to investors parking in dollars while taking profits on gold, tech and equities.
insights.speaker: Daniel Lacalle
insights.so_what: Dollar strength is partly a by-product of de-risking; it reverses when profit-taking ends or the Fed eases.

insights.claim: Lacalle frames currency competition as a race to lose last: the dollar wins only as the least bad alternative to a euro with redenomination risk, a capital-controlled yuan, and a pound, Swiss franc and yen that lack the liquidity to replace it.
insights.speaker: Daniel Lacalle
insights.so_what: Dollar reserve status holds despite debasement, which is consistent with long-term gold strength.
insights.quote: the monetary world is not a world in which there is a battle to see who wins first but who loses first in the debasement of fiat currencies

insights.claim: Lacalle doubts the dollar will strengthen much further because aggressive dollar appreciation historically triggered crises (yen crisis, French debt crisis, Asian financial crisis, Latin American tequila crisis), and nobody in central banking wants that.
insights.speaker: Daniel Lacalle
insights.so_what: Upside in the DXY may be capped; watch EM and dollar-funding stress as a sign of overshoot.
insights.quote: Will we see the US dollar strengthening a lot further? I doubt it.

insights.claim: Lacalle says the Fed's tightening has engineered a massive contraction in financial conditions that is severely hurting countries that rely on dollar liquidity to finance their currencies and capex.
insights.speaker: Daniel Lacalle
insights.so_what: Dollar-funded economies are vulnerable while Fed policy stays tight.

insights.claim: Lacalle argues today's Fed rate hikes have very limited impact on inflation and inflation expectations but large damage to families and small businesses, and the Fed should rely more on balance-sheet and liquidity tools instead.
insights.speaker: Daniel Lacalle
insights.so_what: Further hikes raise growth/credit risk more than they lower inflation, increasing odds of an eventual pivot.
insights.quote: today's world hiking rates has a very limited impact on inflation and on inflation expectations but a very large impact on the private sector

insights.claim: Lacalle says the Fed cannot combat inflation unless fiscal policy is restrictive, because the Fed cannot print anything the government has not printed earlier.
insights.speaker: Daniel Lacalle
insights.so_what: Fiscal deficits, not Fed rhetoric, are the key inflation variable to watch.
insights.quote: the Fed cannot print anything that the government has not printed earlier

themes.theme: Euro area: stagnation and debasement end game

insights.claim: Lacalle says the EU's interventionist energy, industrial, agriculture, technology and finance policies have failed, and the euro area is stagnating despite negative rates, massive ECB stimulus and the Next Generation fund.
insights.speaker: Daniel Lacalle
insights.so_what: Supports a structural underweight of euro-area growth assets versus US and China.

insights.claim: Lacalle says the EU lacks a technological, energy or financial-sector advantage, though its banks have navigated the situation very well.
insights.speaker: Daniel Lacalle
insights.so_what: European banks may be the relative bright spot within a weak European macro picture.

insights.claim: Lacalle sees hope in voters and businesses pushing back, which could bring political change that starts unwinding Europe's bureaucratic, regulatory and tax burdens.
insights.speaker: Daniel Lacalle
insights.so_what: Political change toward deregulation would be the upside catalyst for European assets.

insights.claim: Responding to Louis Gave's view that France or Italy may be forced out of the euro, Lacalle calls redenomination risk real but very unlikely because TARGET2 imbalances mean a French exit would send Germany into depression and devastate bank and pension balance sheets.
insights.speaker: Daniel Lacalle
insights.so_what: Euro break-up trades are low probability; position for depreciation instead.
insights.quote: France leaving the euro means Germany enters into a depression.

insights.claim: Lacalle estimates a new French franc would be worth about 50 cents on the euro at best, effectively slashing French pensions by 70-80%, and a euro break-up would also hit Japanese pension funds that have bought European debt for yield.
insights.speaker: Daniel Lacalle
insights.so_what: Contagion from a euro break-up would extend to Japan, which is one more reason policymakers will avoid it.

insights.claim: Lacalle calls the euro a 'bull market project' that works when economies grow but not in stagnation, comparing the euro area to the Hotel California: you can check out but never leave.
insights.speaker: Daniel Lacalle
insights.so_what: Euro stress rises in downturns; expect policy to absorb it through the currency.
insights.quote: the euro is a bull market project

insights.claim: Lacalle believes the euro's most probable end game is a much more devalued, debased currency, the least damaging path though one that raises euro-area inflation expectations; he also expects the UK to be forced back toward the EU despite the referendum.
insights.speaker: Daniel Lacalle
insights.so_what: Structural bearish EUR thesis; favors real assets over euro-denominated bonds.
insights.quote: What I see as more probable is that the end game for the euro ends being a much more devaluated currency than it is right now.

insights.claim: Nobody is seeking shelter from uncertainty in euro-area assets such as French bonds, according to Lacalle.
insights.speaker: Daniel Lacalle
insights.so_what: French sovereign debt lacks safe-haven demand, which leaves spreads vulnerable.
insights.quote: Nobody has decided to be sheltering themselves from uncertainty in Euro area assets which would mean hoarding French bonds.

insights.claim: Lacalle views the gold crash as a good buying opportunity: the correction stems from the strong dollar and an ETF-driven 'gold rush' that drifted away from a very tight physical market, while central bank buying and constrained supply keep fundamentals bullish.
insights.speaker: Daniel Lacalle
insights.so_what: Accumulate gold on weakness; the paper/ETF overhang, not physical demand, drove the decline.
insights.quote: the debasement of fiat currencies is not something that is a discussion or an idea or an expectation is a policy

insights.claim: Patrick Ceresna sees no sign of a gold low yet: selling accelerated without bullish momentum divergence, gold implied volatility jumped from 22% to 34%, and the 3,300 area (a 2025 consolidation zone) is the first key support below 3,500.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: Gold buyers may wait for 3,300 or evidence the sell cycle has played out before entering.
insights.quote: here we had a jump from the 22% level on gold volatility up to 34%

themes.theme: Market desk: euro hedge and fragile tape

insights.claim: Patrick Ceresna proposes a call-hedged short on March 2027 CME Euro FX futures with a reference price around 1.10, a 57-pip call premium and a maximum loss of about 140 pips at expiration, to express the euro-depreciation view while capping counter-trend rally risk.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: A defined-risk way to short the euro after a big decline, when 200-300 pip squeezes are likely.
insights.quote: At our proposed call premium of 57 pips, the combined position has a maximum loss of approximately 140 pips at the options expiration.

insights.claim: Ceresna reads the failed follow-through of a 300+ point S&P rally (sparked by Jensen returning as Nvidia CEO, after the VIX hit 40) as a possible bull trap, with semis like AMD back at Friday lows, and leans toward the selling not being over.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: Be cautious buying the dip until rallies show follow-through and broadening participation.
insights.quote: the fact that the market has deteriorated this way um is uh has me leaning to the fact that the selling is not over yet

insights.claim: Ceresna flags 6,900 on the S&P as the critical level; if it fails, a retest of March levels around 6,400-6,500 opens up, and the key question is whether this is a Liberation Day-style washout or the start of a bear market.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: Key levels for risk management: 6,900 support, 6,400-6,500 downside target.

insights.claim: Ceresna says the dollar bull trend is intact, driven by funding stress and flight to safety, with no reversal likely until a macro catalyst such as a Fed pivot.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: Don't fade dollar strength until the Fed blinks.

insights.claim: Ceresna sees an asymmetric long setup in oil after a deep pullback: unless a new bear market is starting, oil is near key support and any renewed geopolitical disruption gives the upside tail a bigger payoff.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: Oil calls or long exposure near support give cheap convexity to a geopolitical flare-up.
insights.quote: the upside right tail actually has a much bigger payoff than downside risk, making oil pretty interesting

insights.claim: Copper fell 21% in 28 days back to its March lows after COT positioning showed copper bulls at the 100th percentile all year, and Ceresna says a squeeze catalyst has not yet emerged.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: Crowded-long washout makes copper interesting for a retracement, likely tied to a broader risk-on rally.
insights.quote: A 21% decline in 28 days returning back to the March lows.

insights.claim: The 10-year Treasury yield fell from 5.35% in October to about 4.85%, which Ceresna links to AI-slowdown growth fears and tighter financial conditions that could push the Fed to signal a pause at the December meeting.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: Falling yields plus market stress raise odds of a dovish December Fed signal; bonds are the trade on a pivot.
